description: Test your knowledge of MI6.1-3 | Central Nervous System Infections.

cards.text: Name the three main routes of CNS invasion in bacterial meningitis.
cards.answer: 1) Haematogenous spread (most common) — bacteria cross BBB from bacteraemia. 2) Direct spread from contiguous infection (otitis media, sinusitis, skull fracture). 3) Iatrogenic/direct inoculation via LP, neurosurgery, or CSF shunts.

tip.tip: Remember HIM: Haematogenous, Iatrogenic, local spread (contiguous)

cards.text: What is the mechanism of CNS damage in bacterial meningitis?
cards.answer: Bacterial cell wall components trigger cytokine release (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6) → BBB disruption → cerebral oedema and raised ICP. PMNLs release proteases and ROS → further tissue damage, producing turbid CSF with high protein and low glucose.

tip.tip: Cytokines break BBB → oedema; PMNLs cause damage → turbid CSF

cards.text: Which organisms commonly cause bacterial meningitis in neonates (0–3 months)?
cards.answer: *Group B Streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae)*, *Escherichia coli* (K1 antigen), and *Listeria monocytogenes*. These differ from older children, where *N. meningitidis* and *S. pneumoniae* predominate.

tip.tip: GBS and E. coli K1 are neonatal classics; Listeria is the 'odd one out' — doesn't need penicillin alone.

cards.text: What are the key CSF findings in tuberculous meningitis (TBM)?
cards.answer: Clear or xanthochromic fluid; lymphocytic pleocytosis (100–400 cells/mm³); very high protein; very low glucose. Cobweb clot on standing (characteristic). AFB smear only 10–40% sensitive; CBNAAT (GeneXpert Ultra) is now first-line rapid test; culture is gold standard (4–6 weeks).

tip.tip: TBM CSF = Xanthochromic, Lymphocytes, Protein UP, Glucose DOWN, Cobweb clot. Use CBNAAT not smear.

cards.text: How do viral and bacterial meningitis differ in CSF glucose levels?
cards.answer: Bacterial meningitis: low CSF glucose (consumed by bacteria and PMNLs). Viral (aseptic) meningitis: normal CSF glucose. This is a key distinguishing feature; TBM also has very low glucose.

tip.tip: Viral = normal glucose (clear CSF). Bacteria/TB = low glucose (turbid/xanthochromic CSF).

cards.text: What is the cause and diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis?
cards.answer: *Cryptococcus neoformans* causes subacute meningitis in immunocompromised patients (HIV CD4 <100, steroids, transplant). CSF shows clear fluid with lymphocytic pleocytosis, elevated protein, and low glucose. Diagnosis: India ink preparation (encapsulated yeasts), but CrAg latex agglutination test is highly sensitive and specific.

tip.tip: Crypto in immunocompromised. India ink shows encapsulated yeast. CrAg test is gold standard diagnosis.

cards.text: Name the most common cause of viral (aseptic) meningitis and its CSF pattern.
cards.answer: Enteroviruses (Coxsackievirus, Echovirus, Enterovirus 71) are most common. CSF: clear, lymphocytic pleocytosis, mildly elevated protein, and **normal glucose** (unlike bacterial/TB). Usually self-limiting; no specific antiviral except HSV (aciclovir).

tip.tip: Viral = Enteroviruses. CSF = Clear, normal glucose, lymphocytes. Self-limiting.

cards.text: How does TBM differ from acute bacterial meningitis in clinical course and CSF presentation?
cards.answer: TBM: subacute/chronic onset (days to weeks), low-grade fever, cranial nerve palsies from basal exudate. CSF: xanthochromic (not turbid), moderate lymphocytic pleocytosis, very high protein, very low glucose, cobweb clot. Bacterial: acute onset, high fever, turbid CSF, very high cell count (mostly PMNLs).

tip.tip: TBM is SLOW (subacute); Bacterial is FAST (acute). TBM CSF is xanthochromic with cobweb clot.
